## Three numbers a risk desk cannot read off an average

A risk officer has to say how much the US equity market might lose next month, and
a strategist in the next room has to say how large the equity premium is. Both
questions are asked of the same series, the monthly excess return on the market
portfolio, and both are usually answered with a sample average and a sample standard
deviation. That answer quietly assumes that returns are Normal, which they are not.
Over the window we use below the monthly excess return has a skewness of $-0.55$ and a
kurtosis of $4.03$ against the Normal's $3$, and the four worst months in the sample
are losses of $17.2\%$, $16.0\%$, $13.4\%$ and $10.7\%$. A Normal fitted to this series
calls a month like October 2008 a once-in-several-centuries event, which is a statement
no risk officer believes.

The standard repair is to let the returns be Student-$t$ rather than Normal, which adds a
third parameter, the degrees of freedom $\nu$, controlling tail thickness. That single
change breaks every closed form we have relied on so far. There is no conjugate prior for
the degrees of freedom, so the posterior of the three parameters has a normalising constant
with no analytic expression, and none of the quantities a desk wants, not the mean premium,
not the probability that tails are thick, not a one-month value at risk, can be written
down. They can only be computed.

This lecture develops the three general ideas that make such a posterior computable:
Monte Carlo integration, which turns integrals into averages of draws; importance
sampling, which uses draws from the wrong distribution and corrects them with weights;
and rejection sampling, which discards enough draws from the wrong distribution that the
survivors are exact draws from the right one. Each is stated as a general result at
arbitrary parameter dimension and then run on one and the same posterior, defined next.
Lectures 4 and 5 attack that identical posterior with Gibbs sampling and with
Metropolis-Hastings, so that every method in the course can be compared on one problem
rather than on five.

## The target: a Student-$t$ model for the equity premium

Write $r_t$ for the monthly excess return on the US market portfolio from the Kenneth
French data library, and take the window from January 1990 to July 2026. The model is

$$
r_t \mid \mu, \sigma, \nu \;\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\; t_\nu(\mu, \sigma),
\qquad t = 1, \dots, n,
$$

with density

$$
f(r_t \mid \mu, \sigma, \nu) =
\frac{\Gamma\!\big(\tfrac{\nu+1}{2}\big)}{\Gamma\!\big(\tfrac{\nu}{2}\big)\sqrt{\pi\nu}\,\sigma}
\left[1 + \frac{1}{\nu}\left(\frac{r_t - \mu}{\sigma}\right)^{\!2}\right]^{-(\nu+1)/2}.
$$

All three parameters mean something. The location $\mu$ is the monthly equity premium,
the scale $\sigma$ sets the size of a typical monthly move, with return standard deviation
$\sigma\sqrt{\nu/(\nu-2)}$ whenever $\nu > 2$, and the degrees of freedom $\nu$ govern
tail thickness: small $\nu$ makes crashes a regular feature, while $\nu$ above about $30$
is indistinguishable from a Normal at this sample size.

The priors are

$$
\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, s_0^2), \qquad
\sigma^2 \sim \text{IG}(\alpha_0, \delta_0), \qquad
\nu - 2 \sim \text{Exp}(1/\bar\nu)\ \text{truncated to } (0, 48],
$$

with $m_0 = 0$, $s_0 = 0.01$, $\alpha_0 = 3$, $\delta_0 = 0.0032$ and $\bar\nu = 10$.
The prior on $\mu$ is centred at zero with a monthly standard deviation of one percent,
agnostic about the sign of the premium but ruling out absurd values. The inverse-Gamma
prior has mean $\delta_0/(\alpha_0 - 1) = 0.0016$, a monthly scale of four percent, and a
shape of three keeps it loose. The prior on $\nu$ is an exponential with mean $10$ shifted
to live on $(2, 50]$: the shift to $2$ makes it proper and keeps the return variance
finite, and the truncation at $50$ keeps $\nu$ where the data can speak, since the
likelihood is nearly flat beyond that point and an unbounded prior would leave a right
tail driven by the prior alone.

Throughout, collect the parameters into $\theta = (\mu, \sigma, \nu)$, so $k = 3$. The
inverse-Gamma follows Lecture 2 and is implemented as
`scipy.stats.invgamma(a=alpha_0, scale=delta_0)`; the notation table at the end bridges
to sources that write it in terms of the precision $h = 1/\sigma^2$.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats, optimize
from scipy.special import gammaln
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})
```

The seed governs only the simulation error of the estimates below. Nothing here is
simulated data: every posterior is conditioned on realised market returns.

```{python}
ff_m = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "ff_factors_monthly.parquet")
sample = ff_m["1990-01":"2026-07"]
r = sample["mkt_rf"].to_numpy()
n = r.size

print(f"{n} months, {sample.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {sample.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(f"mean {r.mean():.5f}  sd {r.std(ddof=1):.5f}  "
      f"skewness {stats.skew(r):.3f}  kurtosis {stats.kurtosis(r, fisher=False):.3f}")
print(f"five worst months: {np.sort(r)[:5].round(3)}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.6))
axes[0].plot(sample.index, r, lw=0.8, color="steelblue")
axes[0].set_xlabel("date"); axes[0].set_ylabel("monthly excess return")
axes[0].set_title(f"Market excess return, {n} months")
grid_r = np.linspace(-0.20, 0.20, 400)
axes[1].hist(r, bins=40, density=True, alpha=0.55, color="steelblue", label="data")
axes[1].plot(grid_r, stats.norm(r.mean(), r.std(ddof=1)).pdf(grid_r), "k--",
             lw=1.5, label="fitted Normal")
axes[1].set_xlabel("monthly excess return"); axes[1].set_ylabel("density")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=9); axes[1].set_title("Tails are thicker than Normal")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The left panel shows the familiar clusters of turbulence around 2000, 2008 and 2020. The
right panel is the reason for the model: the histogram has more mass than the fitted
Normal in the centre and in the far tails and less in the shoulders, which is the
signature of a scale mixture rather than of a single Gaussian, and the Student-$t$ is the
simplest distribution with that shape.

## Posterior summaries are ratios of kernel integrals

Every number we will report is an integral. Writing the prior density as $\phi(\theta)$,
the likelihood as $f(y \mid \theta)$ and the marginal likelihood as $f(y)$, Bayes'
theorem is

$$
\phi(\theta \mid y) = \frac{\phi(\theta) f(y \mid \theta)}{f(y)}
\;\propto\; \phi(\theta) f(y \mid \theta) \;\equiv\; \kappa(\theta \mid y),
$$

where $\kappa(\theta \mid y)$ is a kernel of the posterior, the shape of a density with
the normalising constant left out. Any posterior summary is the expectation of some
function $g(\theta)$, and written with the kernel it becomes

$$
\mathbb{E}[g(\theta) \mid y]
= \int g(\theta)\, \phi(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta
= \frac{\displaystyle\int g(\theta)\, \kappa(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta}
       {\displaystyle\int \kappa(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta},
$$

because multiplying numerator and denominator by the same missing constant
$K(y) = \int \kappa(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta$ leaves the ratio unchanged, and the
denominator is the special case $g(\theta) = 1$. Choosing $g(\theta) = \mu$ gives the
posterior mean premium, $g(\theta) = \mathbf{1}\{\nu < 10\}$ the posterior probability of
genuinely thick tails, and $g(\theta) = \Pr(r_{n+1} < c \mid \theta)$ a predictive tail
probability. Everything below approximates this one ratio without ever computing $K(y)$
on its own.

Two different failures can put this ratio out of analytic reach, and it is worth keeping
them apart. The first is that $K(y)$ itself has no closed form, so we know only the
kernel; the ratio above dispatches exactly that, since it never asks for $K(y)$
separately. The second is that even with a fully known density a particular $g$ may have
no closed-form integral, as with a ratio of two jointly Normal parameters, a well defined
random variable that can nonetheless fail to have a finite mean, exactly as Lecture 2
warned when dividing one regression coefficient by another. Both occur here, and the
methods below handle both at once.

The kernel itself is available in closed form and cheap to evaluate. We code its
logarithm, because the likelihood of $439$ observations is of order $e^{750}$ and would
overflow otherwise.

```{python}
m_0, s_0 = 0.0, 0.01                    # mu ~ N(m_0, s_0^2)
alpha_0, delta_0 = 3.0, 0.0032          # sigma^2 ~ IG(alpha_0, delta_0)
nu_lo, nu_hi, nu_mean = 2.0, 50.0, 10.0 # nu - 2 ~ Exp(1/nu_mean) truncated to (0, 48]
nu_const = -np.log(nu_mean) - np.log(1.0 - np.exp(-(nu_hi - nu_lo) / nu_mean))


def log_prior(mu, sigma, nu):
    """Log joint prior density of (mu, sigma, nu); sigma carries the IG Jacobian 2*sigma."""
    lp = -0.5 * np.log(2 * np.pi * s_0 ** 2) - 0.5 * ((mu - m_0) / s_0) ** 2
    lp = lp + (np.log(2.0 * sigma) + alpha_0 * np.log(delta_0) - gammaln(alpha_0)
               - (alpha_0 + 1) * np.log(sigma ** 2) - delta_0 / sigma ** 2)
    return lp + nu_const - (nu - nu_lo) / nu_mean


def log_lik(mu, sigma, nu):
    """Student-t log likelihood, evaluated in blocks to bound memory."""
    out = np.empty(mu.shape)
    for i in range(0, mu.size, 20_000):
        m, s, v = mu[i:i + 20_000], sigma[i:i + 20_000], nu[i:i + 20_000]
        z2 = ((r[None, :] - m[:, None]) / s[:, None]) ** 2
        out[i:i + 20_000] = (n * (gammaln((v + 1) / 2) - gammaln(v / 2)
                                  - 0.5 * np.log(np.pi * v) - np.log(s))
                             - 0.5 * (v + 1) * np.log1p(z2 / v[:, None]).sum(axis=1))
    return out


def log_kernel(mu, sigma, nu):
    """log kappa(theta | y), minus infinity outside the prior support."""
    mu, sigma, nu = (np.asarray(a, float).ravel()
                     for a in np.broadcast_arrays(mu, sigma, nu))
    out = np.full(mu.shape, -np.inf)
    ok = (sigma > 0) & (nu > nu_lo) & (nu <= nu_hi)
    if ok.any():
        out[ok] = log_lik(mu[ok], sigma[ok], nu[ok]) + log_prior(mu[ok], sigma[ok], nu[ok])
    return out


print(f"log kappa at (0.009, 0.038, 8) = {log_kernel(0.009, 0.038, 8.0)[0]:.3f}")
```

With $k = 3$ parameters we can still afford the brute-force answer, and it is worth buying
once: a product grid gives a reference value for every quantity in the chapter, so each
simulation method can be checked rather than trusted. The grid below uses
$64 \times 64 \times 96$ points, which is $393{,}216$ kernel evaluations. That count is the
point. Lecture 1 warned that a grid costs $G^k$ evaluations, so a five-parameter version at
the same resolution would need about $10^{9}$ evaluations and a ten-parameter one about
$10^{18}$. Grids answer this question and then stop working, permanently, one or two
parameters later.

```{python}
g_mu = np.linspace(0.0015, 0.017, 64)
g_sig = np.linspace(0.029, 0.049, 64)
g_nu = np.linspace(2.02, 50.0, 96)
MU, SG, NU = np.meshgrid(g_mu, g_sig, g_nu, indexing="ij")

log_k_grid = log_kernel(MU, SG, NU).reshape(MU.shape)
p_grid = np.exp(log_k_grid - log_k_grid.max())
p_grid /= p_grid.sum()

grid_mean = np.array([(p_grid * MU).sum(), (p_grid * SG).sum(), (p_grid * NU).sum()])
grid_sd = np.array([np.sqrt((p_grid * MU ** 2).sum() - grid_mean[0] ** 2),
                    np.sqrt((p_grid * SG ** 2).sum() - grid_mean[1] ** 2),
                    np.sqrt((p_grid * NU ** 2).sum() - grid_mean[2] ** 2)])
names = ["mu", "sigma", "nu"]
for nm, m_, s_ in zip(names, grid_mean, grid_sd):
    print(f"grid posterior  E[{nm:>5s} | r] = {m_:9.6f}   sd = {s_:.6f}")
print(f"annualised premium at the posterior mean: {12 * grid_mean[0]:.4f}")
print(f"implied return sd {grid_mean[1]*np.sqrt(grid_mean[2]/(grid_mean[2]-2)):.4f} "
      f"monthly vs sample sd {r.std(ddof=1):.4f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.4))
for ax, X, axis_keep, gr, nm, lab in [
        (axes[0], MU, (1, 2), g_mu, grid_mean[0], r"$\mu$  (monthly premium)"),
        (axes[1], SG, (0, 2), g_sig, grid_mean[1], r"$\sigma$  (monthly scale)"),
        (axes[2], NU, (0, 1), g_nu, grid_mean[2], r"$\nu$  (degrees of freedom)")]:
    marg = p_grid.sum(axis=axis_keep)
    ax.plot(gr, marg / np.trapezoid(marg, gr), color="steelblue")
    ax.axvline(nm, color="grey", ls=":")
    ax.set_xlabel(lab); ax.set_ylabel("density")
axes[2].set_xlim(2, 30)
fig.suptitle("The target posterior: marginals from a 393,216-point grid")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The posterior mean premium is $0.9126\%$ a month, or $10.95\%$ a year, noticeably above
the sample average of $0.745\%$ a month. That gap is the Student-$t$ at work: a Normal
model has to explain the 2008 and 2020 crashes by lowering the mean, while the $t$ model
reads them as tail draws and leaves the central tendency higher. The posterior mean scale
is $0.03776$ and the posterior mean degrees of freedom is $8.60$ with a posterior standard
deviation of $3.93$, so the marginal for $\nu$ is wide and clearly right-skewed. The
implied monthly return standard deviation is $0.0431$ against a sample value of $0.0439$,
so the model is not buying fat tails at the cost of overall spread. The right-skewness of
the $\nu$ marginal is worth noticing now, because it is what breaks the first importance
sampler we try.

## Result: Monte Carlo integration

::: {.callout-important}
## Result: the Monte Carlo estimator, its unbiasedness and its standard error

Let $\theta^{(1)}, \dots, \theta^{(S)}$ be independent draws from a distribution $p$ on
$\mathbb{R}^k$, and let $g: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}$ have
$\mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)] = \mu_g$ and $\operatorname{Var}_p[g(\theta)] = \sigma_g^2 <
\infty$. The Monte Carlo estimator

$$
\hat g_S = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S} g\big(\theta^{(s)}\big)
$$

satisfies, for every $S$ and every dimension $k$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat g_S\big] = \mu_g, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}\big[\hat g_S\big] = \frac{\sigma_g^2}{S}, \qquad
\hat g_S \overset{\text{a.s.}}{\longrightarrow} \mu_g, \qquad
\sqrt{S}\,(\hat g_S - \mu_g) \overset{d}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_g^2).
$$

The Monte Carlo standard error is $\text{MCSE} = \sigma_g/\sqrt{S}$, estimated in
practice by $\hat\sigma_g/\sqrt{S}$ with $\hat\sigma_g$ the sample standard deviation of
the $g(\theta^{(s)})$.
:::

Nothing in that statement mentions $k$. That is why simulation escapes the curse of
dimensionality that sank the grid: the accuracy of $\hat g_S$ depends on the variability
of the single random variable $g(\theta)$, not on the volume of the space $\theta$ lives
in.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Unbiasedness is linearity of expectation together with the fact that each $\theta^{(s)}$
is a draw from $p$:

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat g_S\big]
= \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S \mathbb{E}\big[g(\theta^{(s)})\big]
= \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S \mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)] = \mu_g .
$$

Each term is a scalar expectation, so the argument is indifferent to how many components
$\theta$ has.

For the variance, the terms $g(\theta^{(1)}), \dots, g(\theta^{(S)})$ are independent and
identically distributed, so the variance of a sum is the sum of the variances:

$$
\operatorname{Var}\big[\hat g_S\big]
= \frac{1}{S^2}\sum_{s=1}^S \operatorname{Var}\big[g(\theta^{(s)})\big]
= \frac{1}{S^2}\, S\, \sigma_g^2 = \frac{\sigma_g^2}{S}.
$$

Consistency is the strong law of large numbers applied to the one-dimensional sequence
$g(\theta^{(1)}), g(\theta^{(2)}), \dots$, which is a sequence of numbers whatever the
dimension of the object that produced them. The limiting Normality is the central limit
theorem applied to that same sequence, which is legitimate precisely because $\hat g_S$
is itself an average of independent, identically distributed terms of finite variance.
Replacing $\sigma_g$ by its sample counterpart is justified by Slutsky's theorem, since
$\hat\sigma_g \to \sigma_g$ almost surely.
:::

The $\sqrt{S}$ in the denominator is the single most important practical fact about
simulation. The error shrinks with the square root of the number of draws, so halving the
standard error costs four times as many draws and one extra decimal digit costs a hundred
times as many. The estimator converges, but the rate is unforgiving, and every later
question of the form "how many draws do we need" comes back to this line.

To see the machinery work before the difficulty arrives, apply it to the one distribution
in this model we can sample directly, the prior, two of whose moments are known exactly:
$\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2] = \delta_0/(\alpha_0 - 1) = 0.0016$, and for the truncated shifted
exponential with rate $\lambda = 1/\bar\nu$ on $(2, 2+b]$,

$$
\mathbb{E}[\nu] = 2 + \frac{1}{\lambda} - \frac{b e^{-\lambda b}}{1 - e^{-\lambda b}} .
$$

Drawing from the prior on $\nu$ uses the inverse transform, $\nu = 2 - \bar\nu \log\{1 -
u(1 - e^{-b/\bar\nu})\}$ with $u$ uniform.

```{python}
S_mc = 20_000
mu_pr = rng.normal(m_0, s_0, size=S_mc)
sig_pr = np.sqrt(stats.invgamma(a=alpha_0, scale=delta_0).rvs(size=S_mc, random_state=rng))
u_pr = rng.uniform(size=S_mc)
b_nu = nu_hi - nu_lo
nu_pr = nu_lo - nu_mean * np.log(1.0 - u_pr * (1.0 - np.exp(-b_nu / nu_mean)))

exact_var = delta_0 / (alpha_0 - 1.0)
exact_nu = nu_lo + nu_mean - b_nu * np.exp(-b_nu / nu_mean) / (1 - np.exp(-b_nu / nu_mean))

for lab, draws, exact in [("E[sigma^2]", sig_pr ** 2, exact_var),
                          ("E[nu]      ", nu_pr, exact_nu)]:
    est = draws.mean()
    mcse = draws.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(S_mc)
    print(f"prior {lab}  exact {exact:10.6f}   MC {est:10.6f}   "
          f"MCSE {mcse:.6f}   |error|/MCSE {abs(est - exact) / mcse:.2f}")
```

Both estimates sit within two Monte Carlo standard errors of the exact value, which is
what an unbiased estimator with a correctly computed standard error should do. That
standard error says nothing about the prior, which is fixed; it says how far this
particular average of $20{,}000$ draws might be from the number the draws estimate.
Watching the running average makes the rate visible.

```{python}
run_est = np.cumsum(nu_pr) / np.arange(1, S_mc + 1)
s_axis = np.arange(1, S_mc + 1)
band = 1.96 * nu_pr.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(s_axis)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(s_axis, run_est, lw=1, color="steelblue", label="running MC estimate")
ax.axhline(exact_nu, color="black", lw=1, ls=":", label="exact prior mean")
ax.fill_between(s_axis, exact_nu - band, exact_nu + band, alpha=0.2,
                label=r"exact $\pm\,1.96\times$MCSE")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("number of draws  S (log scale)"); ax.set_ylabel(r"estimate of $E[\nu]$")
ax.set_ylim(exact_nu - 2, exact_nu + 2)
ax.legend(); ax.set_title(r"Monte Carlo error shrinks like $1/\sqrt{S}$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The band narrows steadily and the running average stays inside it without ever settling on
the exact value, which is the result above made concrete. Note how slow the narrowing is
on the logarithmic axis: each factor of ten in $S$ buys a factor of only about three in
accuracy.

All of that assumed we can draw from the distribution we are integrating against. For the
prior we can; for the posterior we cannot, because no generator exists for a distribution
known only up to a constant and belonging to no named family. The next two sections are
the standard ways around that.

## Result: importance sampling

The idea is to rewrite the target expectation as an expectation under a distribution we
can sample, called the proposal or importance density $q$, by multiplying and dividing
inside the integral.

::: {.callout-important}
## Result: the importance sampling identity and the self-normalised estimator

Let $p$ be a density on $\mathbb{R}^k$ and let $q$ be a density with $q(\theta) > 0$
wherever $g(\theta) p(\theta) \neq 0$. Then

$$
\mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)]
= \int g(\theta)\, \frac{p(\theta)}{q(\theta)}\, q(\theta)\, d\theta
= \mathbb{E}_q\big[g(\theta)\, w(\theta)\big],
\qquad w(\theta) = \frac{p(\theta)}{q(\theta)},
$$

exactly, not approximately. If $p$ is known only through a kernel
$\kappa(\theta) = c\, p(\theta)$ with $c$ unknown, then with
$\tilde w^{(s)} = \kappa(\theta^{(s)})/q(\theta^{(s)})$ and
$\theta^{(1)},\dots,\theta^{(S)} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} q$ the self-normalised
estimator

$$
\hat g_S^{\,\text{IS}}
= \frac{\sum_{s=1}^{S} g(\theta^{(s)})\, \tilde w^{(s)}}{\sum_{s=1}^{S} \tilde w^{(s)}}
= \sum_{s=1}^{S} g(\theta^{(s)})\, w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)},
\qquad w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)} = \frac{\tilde w^{(s)}}{\sum_{j} \tilde w^{(j)}},
$$

is biased for every finite $S$, with bias of order $1/S$, but is consistent,
$\hat g_S^{\,\text{IS}} \to \mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)]$ almost surely, and asymptotically
Normal at rate $\sqrt{S}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

The identity is a change of measure. Multiplying and dividing the integrand by $q(\theta)$
is legitimate wherever $q(\theta) > 0$, and the support condition guarantees that the set
where $q(\theta) = 0$ contributes nothing to $\int g p$. Recognising
$g(\theta)\{p(\theta)/q(\theta)\}$ as a function integrated against the density $q$ gives
$\mathbb{E}_q[g w]$. For the self-normalised version, write

$$
\hat A_S = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S g(\theta^{(s)})\, w(\theta^{(s)}), \qquad
\hat B_S = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S w(\theta^{(s)}),
$$

where $w = p/q$ is the weight built from the normalised $p$. Each is an ordinary Monte
Carlo average of independent draws from $q$, so by the previous result $\hat A_S$ is
unbiased and consistent for $\mathbb{E}_q[gw] = \mathbb{E}_p[g]$ and $\hat B_S$ for
$\mathbb{E}_q[w] = \int p = 1$.

The unknown constant $c$ multiplies every $\tilde w^{(s)}$ identically, so it cancels from
the ratio and $\hat g_S^{\,\text{IS}} = \hat A_S / \hat B_S$ exactly. This is where
unbiasedness is lost: the expectation of a ratio is not the ratio of expectations, because
$1/\hat B_S$ is convex in $\hat B_S$ and Jensen's inequality bites. A second-order
expansion of $\hat A_S/\hat B_S$ around $(\mathbb{E}\hat A_S, 1)$ gives

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat g_S^{\,\text{IS}}\big] - \mu_g
= \frac{1}{S}\Big\{\mu_g \operatorname{Var}_q[w] - \operatorname{Cov}_q[gw,\, w]\Big\}
+ O(S^{-2}),
$$

so the bias is of order $1/S$ and vanishes faster than the standard error, which is of
order $S^{-1/2}$.

Consistency survives intact. Both $\hat A_S$ and $\hat B_S$ converge almost surely by the
law of large numbers, $\hat B_S \to 1 \neq 0$, and the map $(a, b) \mapsto a/b$ is
continuous there, so the continuous mapping theorem gives
$\hat g_S^{\,\text{IS}} \to \mu_g/1$ almost surely. The delta method applied to the same
ratio gives $\sqrt{S}(\hat g_S^{\,\text{IS}} - \mu_g) \overset{d}{\to}
\mathcal{N}(0, \tau_g^2)$ with $\tau_g^2 = \operatorname{Var}_q[w(\theta)\{g(\theta) -
\mu_g\}]$, provided that variance is finite. Notice that $\tau_g^2$ involves the weights
quadratically, which is the formal reason uneven weights are expensive.
:::

The practical reading is unglamorous but important. The bias shrinks like $1/S$ while the
spread shrinks like $S^{-1/2}$, so the bias is asymptotically negligible relative to the
noise, but no single run at small $S$ is guaranteed to sit on the truth. The trade is
worth making because working with an unnormalised target is usually the only option.

One technical point saves confusion later. Everything above used a normalised $q$, but in
practice one often knows only a kernel $\iota(\theta) \propto q(\theta)$ with unknown
constant $c_\iota = \int \iota$. Building the weight from $\iota$ changes every weight by
the same factor $c_\iota$, which cancels in the self-normalised ratio, so
$\hat g_S^{\,\text{IS}}$ is unaffected. What changes is that the raw average of such
weights no longer estimates one; it estimates $K(y)/c_\iota$. When $c_\iota$ is known,
that average times $c_\iota$ is therefore an estimator of the marginal likelihood $K(y)$,
which is how Lecture 9 computes model evidence.

Now the choice of $q$. Every requirement on a good proposal follows from keeping
$w = \kappa/q$ well behaved: its support must cover everywhere the target has mass, its
tails must be no lighter than the target's, since a proposal that decays faster sends
$w \to \infty$ in the tail, and it must be cheap to sample. For this posterior the natural
first attempt is a Normal centred at the posterior mode with covariance taken from the
curvature of the log kernel there, the Laplace approximation, inflated a little for
safety.

```{python}
neg_log_kernel = lambda t: -log_kernel(t[0], t[1], t[2])[0]
opt = optimize.minimize(neg_log_kernel, np.array([0.009, 0.038, 8.0]),
                        method="Nelder-Mead",
                        options=dict(xatol=1e-8, fatol=1e-8, maxiter=5000))
theta_hat = opt.x

step = np.array([1e-4, 1e-4, 1e-2])                  # central second differences
H = np.empty((3, 3))
for i in range(3):
    for j in range(3):
        ei, ej = np.zeros(3), np.zeros(3)
        ei[i], ej[j] = step[i], step[j]
        H[i, j] = (neg_log_kernel(theta_hat + ei + ej) - neg_log_kernel(theta_hat + ei - ej)
                   - neg_log_kernel(theta_hat - ei + ej)
                   + neg_log_kernel(theta_hat - ei - ej)) / (4 * step[i] * step[j])
Sigma_hat = np.linalg.inv(H)

print(f"posterior mode:  mu {theta_hat[0]:.6f}  sigma {theta_hat[1]:.6f}  nu {theta_hat[2]:.4f}")
print("Laplace sd:     " + "  ".join(f"{v:.6f}" for v in np.sqrt(np.diag(Sigma_hat))))

S_is = 40_000
q_normal = stats.multivariate_normal(mean=theta_hat, cov=4.0 * Sigma_hat)   # scale inflated 2x
th_n = q_normal.rvs(size=S_is, random_state=rng)

log_w = log_kernel(th_n[:, 0], th_n[:, 1], th_n[:, 2]) - q_normal.logpdf(th_n)
w_n = np.where(np.isfinite(log_w), np.exp(log_w - log_w[np.isfinite(log_w)].max()), 0.0)
w_n /= w_n.sum()

ess_n = 1.0 / np.sum(w_n ** 2)
is_mean_n = w_n @ th_n
print(f"outside the prior support: {np.mean(~np.isfinite(log_w)):.3f} of draws")
for nm, est, tru in zip(names, is_mean_n, grid_mean):
    print(f"IS(Normal)  E[{nm:>5s}] = {est:9.6f}   grid {tru:9.6f}   "
          f"error {est - tru:+.6f}")
print(f"ESS = {ess_n:.0f} out of {S_is} ({100*ess_n/S_is:.1f}%), "
      f"largest normalised weight {w_n.max():.4f}")
```

The estimates for $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are excellent, agreeing with the grid to within a few
parts in ten thousand. The estimate for $\nu$ is not: it comes out at $8.42$ against the
grid value of $8.60$, an error of two percent that no amount of staring at the point
estimate would reveal. The effective sample size, defined next, explains why, and so does the fact
that thirteen percent of the Normal proposal's draws land outside the prior support, at
negative $\sigma$ or at $\nu$ below $2$, and are wasted outright.

## Result: weight variance and the effective sample size

::: {.callout-important}
## Result: why uneven weights inflate the variance, and what ESS measures

For the unnormalised estimator, the second moment of a single weighted term is

$$
\mathbb{E}_q\!\big[\{g(\theta) w(\theta)\}^2\big]
= \int g(\theta)^2 \frac{p(\theta)^2}{q(\theta)^2}\, q(\theta)\, d\theta
= \mathbb{E}_p\!\big[g(\theta)^2\, w(\theta)\big],
$$

so the variance of the importance sampling estimator is inflated exactly where
$w(\theta)$ is large and $g(\theta)^2 p(\theta)$ is not negligible. If $q$ has lighter
tails than $p$ in some direction, then $w(\theta) \to \infty$ along it and the variance
can be infinite even though the estimator remains consistent. The standard one-number
diagnostic is the effective sample size

$$
\text{ESS} = \frac{\big(\sum_{s} \tilde w^{(s)}\big)^2}{\sum_{s} (\tilde w^{(s)})^2}
= \frac{1}{\sum_{s} \big(w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)}\big)^2} \;\in\; [1, S],
$$

which equals $S$ when all normalised weights are $1/S$ and falls towards $1$ as a single
weight comes to dominate. It is the number of independent draws from $p$ that the
weighted sample is worth.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

The second-moment identity is the same change of measure as before, applied to $g^2 w^2$
rather than to $g w$: one factor of $q$ in the denominator cancels against the $q$ from
the expectation, leaving $g^2 w$ integrated against $p$. Subtracting $\mu_g^2$ gives the
variance of a single term, and dividing by $S$ gives the variance of the estimator.

For the effective sample size, compare the variance of the weighted average with that of
an unweighted average of $S_{\text{eff}}$ draws from $p$. Treating the weights as fixed,
$\sum_s w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)} g(\theta^{(s)})$ has variance
$\sigma_g^2 \sum_s (w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)})^2$, while the unweighted average has variance
$\sigma_g^2/S_{\text{eff}}$. Equating them gives
$S_{\text{eff}} = 1/\sum_s (w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)})^2$. The bounds follow from
$\sum_s (w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)})^2 \ge 1/S$ by Cauchy-Schwarz, with equality when all
weights are equal, and $\le 1$, with equality when one weight is one and the rest zero.
:::

Applied to the run above, the ESS is about eight percent of the draws, and the diagnosis
follows from the shape of the posterior. The marginal for $\nu$ is right-skewed with a
long tail towards thirty, while a Normal proposal's tail dies like $e^{-x^2}$. In the
region $\nu \in (15, 40)$, where the posterior still has real mass, the proposal has
almost none, so the few draws that land there carry very large weights, and a right tail
represented by a handful of heavy points is a right tail estimated badly. That is
precisely the $8.42$ against $8.60$.

The repair is to give the proposal heavier tails than the target in every direction, built
component by component: a Student-$t_5$ for $\mu$ and for $\sigma$, whose polynomial tails
dominate the posterior's exponential ones, and for $\nu$ the prior itself. That last choice
is not laziness. Because the likelihood is bounded above by some finite $\bar l$, the kernel
obeys $\kappa(\theta) = l(\theta)\phi(\theta) \le \bar l\, \phi(\theta)$, so a proposal
built from the prior can never have lighter tails than the posterior. It is safe by
construction.

```{python}
q_mu = stats.t(df=5, loc=0.00913, scale=0.0022)
q_sig = stats.t(df=5, loc=0.0378, scale=0.0024)
q_nu = stats.truncexpon(b=(nu_hi - nu_lo) / nu_mean, loc=nu_lo, scale=nu_mean)


def q_rvs(size, generator):
    return np.column_stack([q_mu.rvs(size, random_state=generator),
                            q_sig.rvs(size, random_state=generator),
                            q_nu.rvs(size, random_state=generator)])


def q_logpdf(th):
    return q_mu.logpdf(th[:, 0]) + q_sig.logpdf(th[:, 1]) + q_nu.logpdf(th[:, 2])


th_h = q_rvs(S_is, rng)
log_w_h = log_kernel(th_h[:, 0], th_h[:, 1], th_h[:, 2]) - q_logpdf(th_h)
w_h = np.where(np.isfinite(log_w_h),
               np.exp(log_w_h - log_w_h[np.isfinite(log_w_h)].max()), 0.0)
w_h /= w_h.sum()

ess_h = 1.0 / np.sum(w_h ** 2)
is_mean_h = w_h @ th_h
for nm, est, tru in zip(names, is_mean_h, grid_mean):
    print(f"IS(heavy)   E[{nm:>5s}] = {est:9.6f}   grid {tru:9.6f}   "
          f"error {est - tru:+.6f}")
print(f"ESS = {ess_h:.0f} out of {S_is} ({100*ess_h/S_is:.1f}%), "
      f"largest normalised weight {w_h.max():.4f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.8))
for ax, ww, ess_, ttl in [(axes[0], w_n, ess_n, "Normal proposal (Laplace, inflated)"),
                          (axes[1], w_h, ess_h, "heavy-tailed proposal")]:
    ax.hist(ww * S_is, bins=60, color="steelblue", alpha=0.85)
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xlabel(r"normalised weight $\times\, S$")
    ax.set_title(f"{ttl}\nESS = {ess_:.0f} of {S_is}  ({100*ess_/S_is:.1f}%)", fontsize=10)
axes[0].set_ylabel("count (log scale)")
fig.suptitle("Importance weights on the Student-t posterior")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The heavier-tailed proposal raises the effective sample size to about thirty percent of
the draws and brings the estimate of $\nu$ to within four hundredths of the grid value.
The figure shows why. Both weight distributions are right-skewed, which is normal and not
by itself a problem; what differs is the extreme. The largest single normalised weight
under the Normal proposal is roughly five hundred times the average weight $1/S$, while
under the heavy-tailed proposal it is about eight times. A weight distribution whose
maximum is far out relative to its bulk is the visual form of a small effective sample
size, and it is the thing to look at before believing any importance sampling estimate.

Two habits keep such a run honest. Always plot the weights, and treat a single draw
carrying a large share of the total as a failure of the proposal rather than an accident
of the seed. And track the coefficient of variation of the raw weights,
$\text{sd}(w)/\text{mean}(w)$, as $S$ grows: one that keeps climbing is the signature of
an infinite weight variance and cannot be trusted however large $S$ is made. Note also
that finding heavy enough tails in every direction took a few minutes of thought at
$k = 3$ with a posterior we could plot, and that no fixed $q$ chosen in advance will do at
the $k = 40$ of Lecture 6, which is why Lectures 4 and 5 exist.

## Result: rejection sampling

Importance sampling returns weighted points. Rejection sampling returns actual draws from
the posterior, by discarding proposals geometrically rather than reweighting them.

::: {.callout-important}
## Result: an accepted draw is an exact draw from the target

Let $\kappa$ be a kernel of the target with $K = \int \kappa(\theta)\, d\theta < \infty$
and target density $p = \kappa/K$. Let $q$ be a density and $M$ a constant with

$$
\kappa(\theta) \le M\, q(\theta) \qquad \text{for all } \theta .
$$

Repeat: draw $\tilde\theta \sim q$ and $u \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ independently, and
accept $\theta = \tilde\theta$ if

$$
u \le \frac{\kappa(\tilde\theta)}{M\, q(\tilde\theta)} ,
$$

otherwise discard and start again. Then every accepted $\theta$ is an exact draw from
$p$, accepted draws are mutually independent, and the acceptance probability at any
single trial is

$$
\Pr(\text{accept}) = \frac{K}{M} .
$$

No reweighting of accepted draws is needed, and the expected number of proposals per
accepted draw is $M/K$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Take the joint density of proposing $\tilde\theta$ and accepting it. The proposal has
density $q(\theta)$, and given $\tilde\theta = \theta$ the acceptance event has
probability $\kappa(\theta)/\{M q(\theta)\}$ because $u$ is uniform on $(0,1)$ and the
envelope condition guarantees the ratio lies in $[0,1]$. Hence

$$
\Pr(\text{propose near }\theta \text{ and accept})
= q(\theta)\, \frac{\kappa(\theta)}{M q(\theta)} = \frac{\kappa(\theta)}{M} .
$$

Integrating over $\theta$ gives the unconditional acceptance probability
$\int \kappa(\theta)\, d\theta / M = K/M$. Dividing the joint density by that
probability gives the density of an accepted draw,

$$
p(\theta \mid \text{accept}) = \frac{\kappa(\theta)/M}{K/M}
= \frac{\kappa(\theta)}{K} = p(\theta),
$$

which is the target exactly, with the unknown constant $K$ cancelling. Independence of
successive accepted draws follows because the trials are independent and the accept
decision depends only on the current trial.

Geometrically the same argument reads as an area statement. The first two steps generate a
point uniformly over the region under the envelope,
$\{(\theta, v) : 0 \le v \le M q(\theta)\}$, since $\theta$ comes from $q$ and
$v = u M q(\theta)$ is uniform on $[0, M q(\theta)]$ given $\theta$. The third keeps the
points that also fall under $\kappa$, a sub-region of the envelope. A point uniform on a
region and restricted to a sub-region is uniform on that sub-region, and the marginal of
$\theta$ under a uniform distribution on the area beneath a curve is the density
proportional to that curve. The acceptance probability is the ratio of the two areas, and
when $q = p$ exactly $M = 1$ and everything is accepted.
:::

The envelope constant is the whole practical problem. We need an $M \ge
\sup_\theta \kappa(\theta)/q(\theta)$, and we reuse the heavy-tailed proposal, whose
tails dominate the target's in every direction so that the supremum is finite. We locate
it numerically, over the evaluation grid and over a large sample from $q$, which is
reliable here only because $k = 3$ and the posterior is unimodal. In higher dimensions a
numerically located envelope is a trap, and this is one reason rejection sampling is
rarely used on large models.

```{python}
grid_pts = np.column_stack([MU.ravel(), SG.ravel(), NU.ravel()])
probe = q_rvs(300_000, rng)
log_ratio = np.concatenate([
    log_k_grid.ravel() - q_logpdf(grid_pts),
    log_kernel(probe[:, 0], probe[:, 1], probe[:, 2]) - q_logpdf(probe)])
log_M = np.nanmax(log_ratio[np.isfinite(log_ratio)])

cell = (g_mu[1] - g_mu[0]) * (g_sig[1] - g_sig[0]) * (g_nu[1] - g_nu[0])
log_K = np.log(np.exp(log_k_grid - log_k_grid.max()).sum() * cell) + log_k_grid.max()
print(f"log K (grid) = {log_K:.3f},  log M = {log_M:.3f}")
print(f"theoretical acceptance rate K/M = {np.exp(log_K - log_M):.4f}")

N_want, kept, n_tried = 20_000, [], 0
while sum(a.shape[0] for a in kept) < N_want:
    cand = q_rvs(40_000, rng)
    log_u = np.log(rng.uniform(size=cand.shape[0]))
    acc = log_u <= (log_kernel(cand[:, 0], cand[:, 1], cand[:, 2])
                    - q_logpdf(cand) - log_M)
    kept.append(cand[acc])
    n_tried += cand.shape[0]

post = np.vstack(kept)
print(f"observed acceptance rate {post.shape[0] / n_tried:.4f} "
      f"({post.shape[0]} accepted from {n_tried} proposals)")
post = post[:N_want]

for j, nm in enumerate(names):
    est, mcse = post[:, j].mean(), post[:, j].std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(N_want)
    print(f"rejection  E[{nm:>5s}] = {est:9.6f}  MCSE {mcse:.6f}  "
          f"grid {grid_mean[j]:9.6f}  |error|/MCSE {abs(est-grid_mean[j])/mcse:.2f}")
p_thick = (post[:, 2] < 10).mean()
print(f"P(nu < 10 | r) = {p_thick:.4f}  "
      f"(MCSE {np.sqrt(p_thick*(1-p_thick)/N_want):.4f})")
```

The observed acceptance rate agrees with the theoretical $K/M$ to within two
ten-thousandths, a check on both the envelope and the arithmetic, and the three posterior
means land within about one Monte Carlo standard error of the grid values. We now have
$20{,}000$ independent, unweighted draws from the posterior, usable downstream exactly like
draws from a named distribution. The price is the acceptance rate, roughly ten proposals
per draw kept, which is tolerable here. In $k$ dimensions the volume between a safe
envelope and the target typically makes $M/K$ grow exponentially in $k$, so rejection
sampling suffers from the same curse of dimensionality as the grid, just with a slower
fuse.

One special case deserves naming because it recurs throughout the course. Suppose the
target is an unrestricted posterior with kernel $\kappa(\theta)$ truncated to a region
$\Theta_r$, and the unrestricted posterior is already easy to simulate. Then it serves as
its own proposal with envelope constant exactly $M = 1$, since
$\kappa(\theta)\mathbf{1}\{\theta \in \Theta_r\} \le 1 \cdot \kappa(\theta)$ holds
trivially, and the algorithm collapses to drawing from the unrestricted posterior and
discarding whatever falls outside $\Theta_r$. The acceptance rate is then
$\Pr(\theta \in \Theta_r \mid y)$, usually a quantity of interest in its own right. This
is how sign restrictions are imposed in the structural vector autoregressions of Lecture
7, and the curse of dimensionality returns in a new guise: restricting several components
at once shrinks the accepted region multiplicatively.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.8))
marg_nu = p_grid.sum(axis=(0, 1))
axes[0].hist(post[:, 2], bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.6, color="steelblue",
             label="rejection draws")
axes[0].plot(g_nu, marg_nu / np.trapezoid(marg_nu, g_nu), "k-", lw=1.6,
             label="grid marginal")
axes[0].set_xlim(2, 30); axes[0].set_xlabel(r"$\nu$"); axes[0].set_ylabel("density")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=9); axes[0].set_title(r"Exact draws reproduce the $\nu$ marginal")
axes[1].scatter(post[:, 1], post[:, 2], s=3, alpha=0.12, color="steelblue")
axes[1].set_xlabel(r"$\sigma$"); axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\nu$"); axes[1].set_ylim(2, 30)
axes[1].set_title(r"Joint posterior of $(\sigma, \nu)$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The left panel confirms that the accepted draws reproduce the grid marginal for $\nu$ with
no weight appearing anywhere in the calculation. The right panel explains the importance
sampling failure diagnosed earlier: $\sigma$ and $\nu$ are strongly positively dependent
and the cloud curves upwards, because a model with thicker tails needs a smaller scale to
fit the same data. An elliptical Normal proposal cannot follow a curved ridge, so it
wastes draws on one side and starves the other.

## Sampling importance resampling

Importance sampling gives weighted points and rejection sampling gives unweighted points
at a cost that grows quickly with dimension. Sampling importance resampling, or SIR, is
the cheap compromise. Having drawn $\theta^{(1)}, \dots, \theta^{(S)} \sim q$ with
normalised weights $w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)}$, draw $N \le S$ indices from $\{1, \dots, S\}$
with replacement using the weights as selection probabilities and keep the corresponding
$\theta$ values. A heavily weighted draw is copied more often and a negligible one is
unlikely to appear, so the resampled set is approximately an unweighted sample from $p$.
The approximation is exact only as $S \to \infty$ with $N$ fixed, which is the essential
difference from rejection sampling, but it needs no envelope constant and wastes no
draws.

```{python}
idx = rng.choice(S_is, size=N_want, replace=True, p=w_n)
sir = th_n[idx]
for j, nm in enumerate(names):
    print(f"SIR from the Normal proposal  E[{nm:>5s}] = {sir[:, j].mean():9.6f}   "
          f"grid {grid_mean[j]:9.6f}")
print(f"distinct source draws used: {np.unique(idx).size} of {S_is}")
```

The resampled means inherit exactly the strengths and the weakness of the weighted sample
they came from: $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are right and $\nu$ is still too low, because resampling
cannot manufacture information the proposal never collected. The number of distinct source
draws is the practical warning signal: the $20{,}000$ resampled points are built from only
$10{,}350$ distinct values, and with a badly degenerate weight distribution the same recipe
would copy a handful of dominant points over and over. SIR is also the bridge to the next
two lectures, where instead of reweighting a fixed proposal once the sampler moves its own
proposal as it goes.

## Application: one-month value at risk

We close by putting the finished posterior to the use that motivated the chapter. The risk
officer wants the loss exceeded with probability one percent next month, and the correct
object is the posterior predictive distribution, which integrates over parameter
uncertainty,

$$
f(r_{n+1} \mid r) = \int f(r_{n+1} \mid \theta)\, \phi(\theta \mid r)\, d\theta ,
$$

and is approximated by drawing one future return per posterior draw: for each accepted
$\theta^{(s)} = (\mu^{(s)}, \sigma^{(s)}, \nu^{(s)})$ take
$r_{n+1}^{(s)} = \mu^{(s)} + \sigma^{(s)} \varepsilon^{(s)}$ with
$\varepsilon^{(s)} \sim t_{\nu^{(s)}}(0,1)$. Value at risk is the empirical quantile of
those draws, which is Monte Carlo integration again with
$g(\theta) = \mathbf{1}\{r_{n+1} < c\}$ and the threshold solved for. We compare three
conventions: this predictive quantile, the plug-in Student-$t$ quantile that fixes
$\theta$ at its posterior mean, and the Normal convention a desk would use by default.

```{python}
eps = stats.t(df=post[:, 2]).rvs(size=N_want, random_state=rng)
r_pred = post[:, 0] + post[:, 1] * eps

mu_b, sig_b, nu_b = post.mean(axis=0)
rows = []
for level in (0.95, 0.99, 0.995):
    a = 1 - level
    predictive = -np.quantile(r_pred, a)
    plug_t = -(mu_b + sig_b * stats.t(df=nu_b).ppf(a))
    normal = -(r.mean() + r.std(ddof=1) * stats.norm.ppf(a))
    rows.append({"level": level, "predictive": predictive, "plug-in t": plug_t,
                 "Normal": normal, "pred - plug-in": predictive - plug_t,
                 "pred - Normal": predictive - normal})
var_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("level")
print((100 * var_table).round(3).to_string() + "   (percent of notional)")
print(f"\nexpected shortfall at 99%: {-r_pred[r_pred < np.quantile(r_pred, 0.01)].mean():.4f}")
print(f"predictive sd {r_pred.std(ddof=1):.4f} vs sample sd {r.std(ddof=1):.4f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(r_pred, bins=120, density=True, range=(-0.30, 0.25), alpha=0.55,
        color="steelblue", label="posterior predictive")
ax.hist(r, bins=40, density=True, histtype="step", lw=1.6, color="black",
        label="realised returns")
for level, colour in ((0.99, "firebrick"), (0.95, "darkorange")):
    ax.axvline(np.quantile(r_pred, 1 - level), color=colour, ls="--",
               label=f"predictive VaR {level:.0%}")
ax.set_xlabel("one-month excess return"); ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.set_title("Predictive distribution and value at risk")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

At the ninety-nine percent level the predictive value at risk is $10.35\%$ of notional,
the plug-in Student-$t$ figure is $9.85\%$ and the Normal figure is $9.47\%$. The Normal
convention gives the smallest number because it has no tail to speak of, and the $0.87$
percentage point gap to the predictive answer is the cost of pretending the four worst
months in the sample were not there. The plug-in Student-$t$ sits between: it has the fat
tail, but it fixes $\nu$ at its posterior mean of $8.57$ and ignores the posterior's own
statement that $\nu$ could be as low as four, the 2.5th percentile of its marginal, which
is where the tail is heaviest. Averaging over the posterior of $\nu$ rather than fixing it
adds the remaining half a percentage point. The gap to the Normal convention grows
monotonically with the level, from $-0.23$ points at ninety-five percent to $0.87$ at
ninety-nine and $1.43$ at ninety-nine and a half.

Two qualifications belong with the number. The model assumes returns are independent and
identically distributed over thirty-six years, which the volatility clustering in the
first figure plainly contradicts, and Lecture 12 replaces exactly this specification with
stochastic volatility. And the predictive distribution carries parameter uncertainty, not
model uncertainty, which is the subject of Lectures 9 and 11.

## Takeaways

Posterior summaries are ratios of kernel integrals, and outside conjugate models those
integrals have no closed form, with grid quadrature failing exponentially fast in the
number of parameters. Monte Carlo integration replaces an integral by an average of
draws, unbiased by linearity of expectation, consistent by the law of large numbers, and
carrying an error of order $1/\sqrt{S}$ regardless of dimension. When the target cannot be
sampled, importance sampling reweights draws from a proposal by the exact ratio of target
to proposal density, and its self-normalised version trades an $O(1/S)$ bias for the
ability to work with an unnormalised kernel; its reliability rests on the proposal having
heavier tails than the target, which the effective sample size measures in one number. On
this posterior a Laplace-based Normal proposal returned an effective sample size of about
eight percent of the draws and an estimate of $\nu$ wrong by two percent, while a proposal
built with deliberately heavy tails reached about thirty percent and got $\nu$ right.
Rejection sampling takes the other route, accepting or discarding proposals geometrically
so that survivors are exact draws from the target, at a known acceptance rate $K/M$ that
matched the observed rate to three decimal places here and that collapses exponentially in
higher dimensions. Sampling importance resampling converts a weighted sample into an
approximately unweighted one and inherits whatever the weights were worth.

Lecture 4 returns to this exact posterior and shows that writing the Student-$t$ as a
Normal scale mixture, $r_t \mid \mu, \sigma, \nu, w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/w_t)$
with $w_t \sim \text{Gamma}(\nu/2, \nu/2)$, makes every full conditional recognisable and
hands us a Gibbs sampler. Lecture 5 attacks it again without the latent variables and
closes with one table of effective sample size per second for every method in Lectures 3
to 5 on this identical problem.

## Reading these results in the sources' notation

The simulation literature uses different letters for the same objects, so it is worth
bridging them once.

| This course | Source (Bauwens, Lopes) | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| posterior kernel, `log_kernel` | kernel $\kappa(\theta \mid y)$ | identical object |
| proposal density $q$, `q_logpdf` | importance function $\iota(\theta)$ | identical object |
| weight $w(\theta) = \kappa(\theta)/q(\theta)$ | $w(\theta) = \kappa(\theta\mid y)/\iota(\theta)$ | identical |
| envelope constant $M$ | $c \ge \sup_\theta \kappa(\theta)/\iota(\theta)$ | identical |
| normalising constant $K(y)$ | marginal likelihood $f(y)$ | identical |
| effective sample size | the weights' histogram and coefficient of variation | ESS summarises the same diagnostic in one number |
| $\sigma^2 \sim \text{IG}(\alpha_0, \delta_0)$ | $h = 1/\sigma^2 \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha_0, 1/\delta_0)$, or $\text{IG}_2(\nu_0, s_0)$ | $\nu_0 = 2\alpha_0$, $s_0 = 2\delta_0$ |

: Notation bridge {.striped}

## Reading guide and sources

Supplied UPM Class 3 for Monte Carlo, importance sampling and rejection sampling.
Geweke (2005), Sections 4.2 to 4.4, and Greenberg (2008), Chapter 5, develop the
integration and simulation arguments. The Student-$t$ location-scale model with unknown
degrees of freedom is treated in Geweke (1993). The UPM materials are by Audronė
Virbickaitė and Martina Zaharieva, adapted to this course's notation and weekly
sequence.

## References

Geweke (1989). Geweke (1993), Bayesian treatment of the independent Student-$t$ linear
model. Robert and Casella, *Monte Carlo Statistical Methods*.
